title: The impact of GLP-1 receptor agonists on chemotherapeutic efficacy: insights from GWAS and experiments.
abstract: Emerging evidence highlights the anti-tumor properties of Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs). However, their synergistic potential with standard chemotherapy remains largely unexplored. Data from Genome-wide association study (GWAS) were used to select single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) strongly associated with lipid-lowering drug targets as instrumental variables. Causal effects were assessed primarily using the inverse variance weighted (IVW) method, supported by comprehensive sensitivity analyses to control for pleiotropy and heterogeneity. These Mendelian randomization (MR) findings were further validated through in vitro functional assays (cell viability, apoptosis, and Western blot) and an in vivo tumor-bearing mouse model. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) activity showed a significantly positive causal relationship with dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR; β = 0.323, P = 6.02 × 10-17) and apoptosis regulator Bcl-2 (β = 0.259, P = 2.1 × 10-11) but a negative relationship with ribonucleoside-diphosphate reductase large subunit (RRM1; β = -0.12, P = 2.32 × 10-3). Functional experiments validated these genetic findings. GLP-1RA significantly enhanced the antitumoral efficacy of gemcitabine both in vitro and in vivo by repressing RRM1. Conversely, GLP-1RA attenuated the anti-tumor effects of methotrexate and paclitaxel by upregulating DHFR and Bcl-2, respectively. Notably, GLP-1RA combination therapy achieved these modulatory effects without exacerbating chemotherapy-associated systemic toxicity. GLP1-RAs can influence the efficacy of chemotherapeutic drugs such as methotrexate, paclitaxel, and gemcitabine.

title: Evasion of Hepatic ILC1 Immunosurveillance Drives Breast Cancer Liver Metastasis.
journal: bioRxiv : the preprint server for biology
abstract: Metastasis, the dissemination of cancer cells to distant organs, is an inefficient process 1 , yet remains the leading cause of cancer-related mortality 2 . The cellular barriers and evasion mechanisms governing organ-specific susceptibility remain incompletely understood 3-5 , hindering the development of effective anti-metastatic therapies 6 . Here, we show that liver-resident type 1 innate lymphoid cells (ILC1s) constitute an essential immunosurveillance barrier against breast cancer liver metastasis that can be bypassed through either cancer cell-intrinsic or host-dependent mechanisms. In a cohort of patients with multi-organ metastatic breast cancer, liver metastasis occurred later and was associated with poorer survival than lung metastasis, with elevated body mass index emerging as a clinical risk factor. This metabolic vulnerability was recapitulated in mice, where a high-fat diet induced hepatosteatosis and selectively enhanced breast cancer colonization of the liver. Mechanistically, liver and lung colonization were restrained by ILC1s and circulating natural killer (NK) cells, respectively. Following cancer cell challenge, NK cells expanded and became activated, clearing cancer cells through the lytic granule pathway and engagement of the death receptor DR5, whereas activated ILC1s selectively required high DR5 expression on cancer cells, supported by AP-2α (TFAP2A)-mediated transcriptional activation, for effective immunosurveillance. Heterozygous copy-number deletion at TNFRSF10B (encoding DR5) in human tumours reduced DR5 expression and predisposed to liver metastasis. Hepatosteatosis further compromised this barrier by reducing IL-15 expression in macrophages, thereby depleting hepatic ILC1s, effects reversible with glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists. Thus, hepatic ILC1s form a critical organ-specific barrier to breast cancer metastasis, vulnerable to both cancer cell-intrinsic DR5 downregulation and host metabolic dysfunction, the latter of which is pharmacologically correctible.

title: Glucagon-like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists and Thyroid Cancer: Review of Preclinical and Human Data.
abstract: Preclinical rodent studies showing a dose-dependent increase in thyroid C-cell hyperplasia and neoplasia with Glucagon-like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists (GLP-1RAs), led the United States Federal Drug Administration to require a boxed warning contraindicating GLP-1RAs for patients with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) or in patients with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome. However, neither primate oncogenicity studies nor patient clinical trials showed C-cell stimulation, calling into question the relevance of rodent models to humans. Indeed, rodents have a high rate of spontaneous thyroid C-cell tumors, a higher number of thyroid C-cells and GLP-1 receptors and use a different pathway from humans in MTC oncogenesis. Although, the majority of meta-analyses of randomized clinical trials and cohort studies using administrative, electronic medical record and/or registry databases report no clear association between GLP-1RA use and thyroid cancer development, pharmacovigilance database studies do demonstrate a positive relationship; however, this association can only be inferred as a possible signal rather than causation and is likely due to notoriety or reporting bias. Additionally, analysis of the overall trends of thyroid cancer incidence in the U.S. since the release of GLP-1RAs for patient use in 2005 show an early increase, probably due to overdiagnosis of papillary carcinoma (PTC); however, the relative proportion of MTC has actually decreased. Because the preponderance of data does not support a causative relationship between GLP-1RA use and MTC (or PTC), we conclude that the need for the boxed warning about the risk of C-cell neoplasia is no longer necessary.

title: Rethinking endpoints for anti-obesity pharmacotherapy in patients with HR+ early breast cancer receiving endocrine therapy: from body weight and BMI to body composition.
abstract: Body weight (BW) and body mass index (BMI) are commonly used to assess obesity and response to weight-management interventions in patients with hormone receptor-positive (HR+) early breast cancer (eBC) receiving endocrine therapy. However, these measures do not adequately reflect changes in fat mass, visceral adiposity, lean mass and sarcopenia-related phenotypes. This focused narrative review examines whether BW and BMI are sufficient endpoints for evaluating obesity management and anti-obesity pharmacotherapy in patients with HR+ eBC receiving endocrine therapy. PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched for relevant evidence until 23 June 2026, including BC-specific studies of obesity pharmacotherapy and registered interventional trials. Studies have reported increases in total and visceral fat mass after adjuvant BC treatment, while changes in lean mass have been less consistent. The identified BC-specific studies remain mainly retrospective and weight-centric, with none assessing body composition as a key outcome. BW and BMI may be useful entry and monitoring variables, but insufficient as stand-alone endpoints. Body composition should be considered as a complementary endpoint, alongside metabolic, functional and oncologic outcomes. Future studies should also assess endocrine therapy adherence and persistence to better characterize the benefits and risks of anti-obesity pharmacotherapy in patients with HR+ eBC.

title: Triaptosis-based biomimetic nanoparticle for the treatment of oral squamous cell carcinoma lymph node metastasis.
abstract: Lymph node metastasis (LNM) is a major determinant of poor prognosis in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) and remains difficult to treat due to the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment and limited response to immune checkpoint blockade. Here, we report a biomimetic nanotherapeutic platform designed to induce triaptosis and enhance antitumor immunity for the treatment of metastatic OSCC. Semaglutide-loaded cerium oxide nanoparticles were engineered and further coated with macrophage membranes to construct Semg@Ce@MM, enabling improved tumor targeting and immune compatibility. The nanoplatform exerts dual therapeutic actions: cerium-mediated pro-oxidative activity triggers VPS34-associated triaptosis characterized by cytoplasmic vacuolization, while semaglutide activates MAPK signaling to enhance tumor cell susceptibility to death. In vitro studies demonstrate potent antitumor activity, including inhibition of tumor cell proliferation and invasion. In a lymph node metastasis model, Semg@Ce@MM significantly suppresses metastatic tumor growth, promotes dendritic cell maturation, increases CD4+ and CD8+ T cell infiltration, and reprograms tumor-associated macrophages toward a pro-inflammatory phenotype. Importantly, Semg@Ce@MM synergizes with anti-PD-L1 therapy to overcome resistance to immune checkpoint blockade while maintaining favorable biosafety. This work establishes a triaptosis-based nanomedicine strategy for the treatment of metastatic OSCC and highlights a promising combinatorial approach that integrates oxidative stress mediated cell death with cancer immunotherapy.

title: Context-dependent functions of insulin, IGF, and GLP signaling in inflammatory bowel disease: linking metabolism, immunity, and intestinal homeostasis.
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), encompassing Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, is a chronic relapsing inflammatory disorder of the gastrointestinal tract characterized by dysregulated immune responses, impaired epithelial barrier function, and alterations in the gut microbiota. Although considerable progress has been made in understanding the immunopathogenesis of IBD, increasing evidence indicates that metabolic signaling pathways are integral regulators of intestinal inflammation, tissue repair, and disease progression. Among these, insulin, insulin-like growth factors (IGFs), and glucagon-like peptides (GLPs) constitute an interconnected immunometabolic network that links nutrient sensing, energy metabolism, epithelial regeneration, and immune homeostasis. Insulin signaling plays context-dependent roles in IBD by regulating glucose metabolism, epithelial repair, inflammatory responses, and interactions with the gut microbiota and bile acid metabolism. While insulin promotes mucosal healing and barrier restoration in intestinal epithelial cells, excessive activation of insulin signaling in immune cells may exacerbate chronic inflammation through epigenetic and cytokine-mediated mechanisms. The IGF axis is also profoundly altered during active IBD, with systemic suppression of IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 accompanying disease activity, whereas local IGF signaling promotes epithelial regeneration, wound healing, and immune regulation. In addition, IGF-binding proteins (IGFBPs) function as active modulators of inflammation, fibrosis, and colitis-associated colorectal cancer in an isoform-specific manner. GLP signaling further integrates metabolism with intestinal immunity; GLP-1 receptor agonists exhibit anti-inflammatory, metabolic, and microbiota-modulating effects, whereas GLP-2 primarily enhances epithelial proliferation, barrier integrity, and mucosal repair. Emerging preclinical and observational clinical studies suggest that GLP-based therapies may improve disease outcomes, although prospective randomized trials are still required. This review summarizes current knowledge regarding the biological functions and molecular mechanisms of insulin, IGFs, IGFBPs, and GLPs in IBD, highlighting their coordinated roles in regulating metabolism, immunity, epithelial homeostasis, and tissue remodeling. A better understanding of these interconnected signaling pathways may facilitate the development of novel immunometabolic therapeutic strategies aimed at promoting mucosal healing, limiting chronic inflammation, and improving long-term outcomes in patients with IBD.

title: The Influence of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists on the Outcomes and Tolerability of Colorectal Cancer Therapies.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) are increasingly being prescribed for metabolic diseases. At times, patients taking GLP-1RAs are also undergoing cancer treatment and surgeries, but their potential interactions with cancer therapies are not well delineated. The purpose of this narrative review is to synthesize the limited pre-clinical, translational, and the clinical evidence available, examining the biological rationale and mechanisms for GLP-1RA-cancer therapy interactions. Oncology research on GLP-1RAs has primarily focused on cancer incidence and survival, yielding generally reassuring safety data and potential outcome improvements. While emerging evidence and biological studies suggest GLP-1RAs could influence treatment tolerance and toxicity, the current clinical data remains limited, observational, and poorly integrated. However, there has been decent mechanistic research that suggests biologically plausible interactions of GLP1-RAs and cancer therapies, specifically through the AMPK and mTOR pathways. The available clinical evidence suggests that GLP-1 receptor agonist use is associated withimproved survival outcomes and reduced treatment-related complications among patients with colorectalcancer receiving chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or surgery. However, these findings are mostlyobservational, and conflicting preclinical evidence highlights the need for prospective studies to clarifythe underlying mechanisms, establish causality, and determine the clinical implications of theseinteractions.

title: Incretin-Based Therapies in Prostate Cancer: From Metabolic Protection to Potential Antitumour Activity - A Narrative Review.
abstract: This narrative review evaluates the clinical rationale for integrating incretin-based therapies as therapeutic adjuncts for men with advanced prostate cancer undergoing androgen axis suppression. Androgen deprivation therapy combined with potent androgen receptor pathway inhibitors significantly prolongs survival but induces severe, progressive metabolic toxicities, including sarcopenic obesity, profound insulin resistance, dyslipidemia, and heightened cardiovascular mortality. To address this unmet need, this study reviews published preclinical mechanisms, epidemiological data, and emerging clinical datasets examining glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and dual glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists. The compiled evidence indicates that these agents provide robust metabolic protection by counteracting treatment-induced metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular risk. Furthermore, incretins may exert indirect antitumor effects by attenuating systemic hyperinsulinemia and visceral adiposity-driven chronic inflammation. Direct antitumor activity is also supported by preclinical evidence demonstrating that receptor engagement on malignant cells downregulates oncogenic signaling pathways, which correlates with recent retrospective clinical database trends showing a numerical reduction in metastatic stage migration among men with localized disease. However, dual receptor agonism introduces mechanistic uncertainty due to potential proliferative signaling cascades in neuroendocrine tumor phenotypes. In conclusion, incretin-based therapies offer a highly rational dual-action strategy for metabolic rescue and potential tumor suppression in advanced prostate cancer. Although several early-phase prospective clinical trials are currently underway to evaluate safety and metabolic efficacy, routine clinical implementation cannot be recommended until rigorously designed randomized controlled trials definitively establish long-term safety, optimal patient selection, and durable oncological outcomes.

title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists and Obesity-Related Cancer by Diabetes Severity.
Management of Obesity in Special Populations and Limited-Resource Settings: An Egyptian Medical Position Statement.
journal: Diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity : targets and therapy
abstract: Obesity/adiposity-based chronic disease is a chronic progressive relapsing disease linked to several comorbidities, with rising prevalence in Egypt. Limited local guidelines and healthcare challenges necessitate evidence-based, culturally adapted strategies. The Egyptian Medical Association for the Study of Obesity convened a clinical multidisciplinary panel to develop consensus recommendations. Evidence was synthesized from literature, prioritizing resource-limited settings and special situations. Assessment: Move beyond Body Mass Index to include waist circumference, waist/height ratio, body composition, and screening for obesity-related complications and diseases. Lifestyle Interventions: a-Nutrition: Mediterranean/dietary approach to stop hypertension diets, slow eating, and supervised fasting (eg Ramadan and Christian). b-Activity: Culturally tailored approaches (eg prayer-time movement and Arabic apps). c-Behavior: Cognitive-behavioral therapy and family-inclusive support. Pharmacotherapy: Use of approved agents (orlistat, naltrexone/bupropion, liraglutide, semaglutide, and tirzepatide) according to obesity-related complications and diseases and age group. Avoid GLP-1, GLP-1/GIP analogues in patients with medullary thyroid cancer, and all agents during pregnancy. Bariatric Surgery: Indicated for body mass index ≥40 kg/m2 (or ≥35 with obesity-related complications and diseases), with lifelong micronutrient supplementation. Special Populations: a-Adolescents: Focus on growth, not only weight-loss; consider pharmacotherapy in different age groups. b-Elderly: Prioritize muscle preservation; avoid weight loss unless obesity-related complications and diseases exist. c-Pregnancy: No weight loss; delay postpartum interventions until lactation is established. Policy Actions: Mandate food labeling, tax sugar-sweetened beverages, and integrate obesity services into primary healthcare. These recommendations provide a pragmatic framework for obesity/adiposity-based chronic disease management in Egypt, emphasizing affordable, patient-centered care, and clinical multidisciplinary collaboration and policy support.

title: Trends in use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists in obese patients with endometrial cancer.
abstract: Most endometrial cancers (EC) are obesity-related; yet, there is little known about utilization of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RAs), which are effective weight loss medications, in EC. This is a retrospective cohort study using TriNetX US Collaborative Network, a de-identified, longitudinal electronic health record dataset. Female patients were identified from 1/1/2018-4/15/2024 with BMI ≥30 and grouped by presence or absence of EC diagnosis. Patients were followed for two years or up to 4/15/26, whichever came first. These two groups were 1:1 propensity score matched for demographics, BMI, and comorbidities. Patients with prior bariatric surgery or GLP-1RA use were excluded. The primary outcome was GLP-1RA use. Subgroup analysis was conducted among patients with BMI ≥40. From 2018 to 2024, GLP-1RAs use in both cohorts increased. However, utilization was consistently lower among patients with EC. In 2018, GLP-1RA use was 1.0% among patients with EC vs. 1.2% among those without EC (RR 0.82, CI 0.60-1.13). By 2024, use increased to 7.8% and 10.6%, respectively (RR 0.73, CI 0.61-0.87). Similar findings were observed among patients with a BMI ≥40, with significantly faster uptake of GLP-1RAs among women without EC. Patients with EC were less likely to receive GLP-1RAs than matched patients without EC despite obesity being a major risk factor for EC. These findings highlight a potential gap in obesity management among EC survivors and support further investigation of the safety and efficacy of GLP-1RAs in this population.

title: Malignant Left Ventricular Hypertrophy: a Dynamic High-Risk Pre-Heart Failure Phenotype.
abstract: To review malignant left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) as a dynamic, higher-risk phenotype within Stage B/pre-heart failure (HF), with a focus on its underlying biology, prognostic significance, and potential modifiability. The malignant LVH phenotype has been newly recognized to be associated with atrial fibrillation, stroke, and cognitive impairment. Recent data also suggest that intensive BP lowering may reduce incident malignant LVH and potentially promote phenotype regression. Other novel approaches that have been shown to reduce adverse remodeling in related populations include direct antifibrotic agents, incretin-analogues, and repurposing known HF therapies. The identification of malignant LVH with a structural and biomarker-based framework may identify a subgroup at particularly high risk for progression to symptomatic HF or CV death.

title: Metabolic oncology: clonal selection and the pre-existing origins of cancer resistance.
abstract: Treatment resistance remains the principal cause of cancer mortality, conventionally modeled as an adaptive response arising under therapeutic pressure. However, a substantial component of resistance is plausibly established before therapeutic exposure, determined by the metabolic environment of the tissue in which the malignancy arises. This article advances the hypothesis that chronic metabolic dysregulation constitutes a selective pressure acting on premalignant tissue. Hyperinsulinemia and increased bioavailable IGF-1 sustain PI3K-AKT-mTOR and RAS-MAPK signaling in tissues where insulin resistance has preserved mitogenic sensitivity, creating an environment permissive to clonal selection. Metabolic intermediates serve as obligate substrates for chromatin-modifying enzymes, coupling metabolic state to the epigenome across the years of subclinical dysregulation that precede diagnosis. Within this landscape, hypoxia stabilizes G9a and promotes locus-specific H3K9 methylation at apoptotic and differentiation loci, whereas one-carbon and S-adenosylmethionine status determine the available H3K9me1 substrate pool. The consequence is an elevated apoptotic threshold and enrichment of epigenetically primed, apoptosis-resistant cells before a tumor is histologically apparent or clinically detected. The argument is fundamentally Darwinian: the metabolic environment selects its survivors before any therapeutic intervention. Clonal dynamics subsequently attributed to therapy may therefore reflect, in part, selection of a pre-existing, resistance-primed population. This is advanced not as an alternative to clonal evolution, of which selection of pre-existing clones is a constituent process, but as a determinant of the pre-treatment resistance heterogeneity upon which therapeutic pressure acts. Existing data on metabolic intervention are discordant, and the discrepancies appear more consistent with differences in intervention potency, timing, and trial design than with failure of the proposed mechanism. Much of the supporting evidence remains indirect and derives from heterogeneous experimental settings. The observations that would distinguish this framework from reverse causation and treatment-induced plasticity are specified, together with its central untested prediction: that pretreatment metabolic state correlates with baseline subclonal architecture, chromatin state, and treatment outcome.

title: Role of glucagon‑like peptide‑1 receptor in cancer: Mechanisms and pharmacologic intervention (Review).
abstract: The glucagon‑like peptide‑1 (GLP‑1) receptor, a G‑protein‑coupled receptor distributed in multiple tissues, can regulate the homeostasis of blood glucose and lipids. GLP‑1 receptor agonist (GLP‑1RA) has been recognized as an effective hypoglycemic drug. The disruption of metabolic processes in diabetes may lead to dysregulation of numerous signaling pathways, thereby promoting the development of malignant tumors. Therefore, the activity of the GLP‑1 receptor may contribute to the development of cancer. Over the years, advancements have been made in understanding the inhibitory effect of GLP‑1RAs on tumorigenesis. Activation of the GLP‑1 receptor can inhibit tumorigenesis by reducing neuroinflammation and oxidative stress, modulating the tumor immune microenvironment and enhancing the chemosensitivity. In addition, GLP‑1RAs also regulate the activity of several related signaling pathways involved in tumorigenesis (such as the AMPK, PI3K/Akt and cAMP/PKA pathways). In the present review, a comprehensive review of the distribution of GLP‑1 receptors and the pharmacological effects of GLP‑1RAs is provided. The intrinsic relationship between GLP‑1 receptors and cancer risk is also discussed, as well as the mechanisms of GLP‑1RAs in inhibiting cancer, with the aim to provide valuable insights for the treatment of cancer using GLP‑1RAs.

title: Urological manifestations in obesity.
journal: Current opinion in endocrinology, diabetes, and obesity
abstract: The global prevalence of obesity continues to rise, with effects ranging across urology. This review summarizes recent evidence on obesity and its impact on various urological conditions, including malignancy, infections, stone disease, functional urology and male reproductive health, chronic kidney disease, and pediatric urology, to guide comprehensive management in this population. Obesity has a paradoxical survival benefit in patients with renal cell carcinoma, while its impact drives aggressive prostate cancer. Obesity increases kidney stone risk, with sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists showing divergent effects on lithogenesis and urinary tract infections. It is a modifiable risk factor for overactive bladder and stress urinary incontinence, both of which improve with weight loss/ bariatric surgery. Robotic surgery mitigates obesity-related perioperative risk. Hypogonadism secondary to obesity is a major reversible cause of male infertility. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA) reverse metabolic hypogonadism and helps in slowing chronic kidney progression. Maternal and childhood obesity may impair testicular descent and can also increase the risk of nocturnal enuresis. Obesity's urological effects are heterogeneous, paradoxical from pediatric to adults, mediated by insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, and hormonal dysregulation. Weight loss and the use of GLP-1 RA may offer a unique strategy for optimizing and treating urological conditions.

title: Semaglutide versus other GLP-1 RAs and cardiovascular risk in obesity-related cancer survivors.
abstract: Obesity-related cancer (ORCa) survivors are a unique population often excluded from landmark GLP-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) trials. Given their cardiovascular risks, we investigated whether semaglutide initiation, compared with other GLP-1 RA, was associated with modified 3-point major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) among ORCa survivors with type 2 diabetes (T2D). We emulated a target trial using PCORnet-UTSW electronic health records (2016-2025). Adults with ORCa and T2D initiating semaglutide versus other GLP-1 RA were included. The primary outcome was modified 3-point MACE (myocardial infarction, stroke, or all-cause mortality). Cumulative incidence risk (CIR), risk difference (RD), and hazard ratio (HR) were estimated in 1:1 propensity score-matched cohort. Among 918 matched patients (semaglutide, n = 459; other GLP-1 RA, n = 459), 124 modified 3-point MACE occurred. The 5-year CIR% was 17.6 (95% CI, 12.3-22.9) for semaglutide and 26.6 (95% CI, 20.7-32.6) for other GLP-1 RA. Semaglutide was associated with lower modified 3-point MACE risk (RD%, -7.41 [95% CI, -11.83 to - 2.98];HR, 0.65 [95% CI, 0.44-0.94]) than other GLP-1 RA. Findings were largely consistent across high-risk subgroups. Semaglutide was associated with a lower modified 3-point MACE risk than other GLP-1 RA. These findings suggest potential heterogeneity in cardioprotective effects and warrant confirmation.

title: Normal-BMI MASLD is Associated with Increased Mortality, Cardiovascular Events, Cancer and Lower GLP-1 Use.
journal: The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism
abstract: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) can occur in individuals who are not overweight or have obesity (normal-BMI MASLD), yet disease burden and management remain poorly characterized. We compared long-term outcomes and incretin-based therapy use between normal-BMI MASLD (nbMASLD) and overweight/obesity-associated MASLD (obMASLD) across racial and ethnic groups. We conducted a retrospective, observational study using the TriNetX United States Network. Adults diagnosed with MASLD or metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) from 2005-2025 were classified using ethnicity-informed normal-BMI thresholds: <23 kg/m2 for Asian, <27 kg/m2 for Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander, and <25 kg/m2 for White/others. Propensity-score matching balanced demographic and clinical covariates. Outcomes were assessed using Kaplan-Meier analyses and Cox proportional hazards models with obMASLD as the reference group. Among 619,171 eligible patients, 51,940 matched pairs were identified. Nb-BMI MASLD was associated with higher all-cause mortality across grouped ethnic groups, with survival of 77.49% versus 83.93% in obMASLD (HR 1.735, CI 1.653-1.822). Ethnicity-specific risks included higher myocardial infarction risk in White and Black patients, higher stroke risk in White patients, higher ESRD risk in Black patients, and increased cancers (colorectal, pancreatic and multiple myeloma) among White patients. Incretin-based therapy (IBT) use was markedly lower in nbMASLD but was associated with improved survival. Patients with nbMASLD demonstrated an increased mortality and ethnicity-specific clinical complications than obMASLD despite a more favorable metabolic profile. These findings demonstrate a potential treatment gap for nbMASLD patients and the shortcomings of BMI-based strategies to risk-stratify MASLD patients.

title: Thyroid surveillance practices in GLP-1 receptor agonist use and its potential influence on thyroid cancer detection: A scoping review.
abstract: Rodent data prompted a boxed warning for medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC) with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs), yet human findings remain inconsistent and may reflect how intensively patients are screened. We mapped reported thyroid screening practices and detection bias reporting. Following JBI methodology and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidance, we searched PubMed, Scopus, Embase, CENTRAL, and ClinicalTrials.gov from 2010 to July 2026. Empirical studies and trial registry records reporting thyroid screening in adult GLP-1RA users were eligible. Records were charted and synthesised descriptively. Thirty-nine records were included (29 published studies, 10 registry records). Screening was predominantly biochemical. Calcitonin was reported in 16/29 studies (55.2%) and all registry records, whereas ultrasonography was reported in 13/29 (44.8%) and no trials. 19/29 studies (65.5%) described a screening protocol. Screening intensity was reported in 18/29 (62.1%) but detection bias in 11/29 (37.9%). All registry records excluded personal or family history of MTC or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 before screening. Thyroid screening in GLP-1RA users is heterogeneous, calcitonin-centred, and inconsistently reported, while patients at highest C-cell risk are excluded from trials. Detection bias is seldom addressed despite documented increases in imaging. Standardised reporting of screening intensity is needed to interpret thyroid cancer rates. OSF Protocol Registration Code: 10.17605/OSF.IO/PEBHS.

title: Methodological Pitfalls in Target Trial Emulations of Incretin Therapeutics and Cancer Endpoints.
GLP-1 RA Prescribing in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes and Cancer.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are increasingly used to treat type 2 diabetes, yet little is known about its utilization patterns in patients with cancer history, given limited oncology-specific guidance. To evaluate trends and factors associated with GLP-1 RA use among Medicare beneficiaries with type 2 diabetes, comparing those with and without cancer history. This retrospective cohort study used Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results-Medicare linked data to identify patients diagnosed with 7 common cancers in 2010 to 2021 and preexisting type 2 diabetes before cancer diagnosis. A noncancer cohort with type 2 diabetes was identified from a 5% random sample of Medicare beneficiaries and matched 1:1 to patients with cancer based on sociodemographic characteristics; controls were assigned a pseudo-index date corresponding to their matched patient's cancer diagnosis date. Beneficiaries were followed up annually until death or December 31, 2022, for TM or December 31, 2021, for MA. Data were analyzed from December 2025 to July 2026. Diagnosis of 1 of 7 common cancers. Any GLP-1 RA use. Proportions of beneficiaries with any GLP-1 RA use annually were stratified by traditional Medicare (TM) and Medicare Advantage (MA). Multivariable logistic regression examined (1) differences in GLP-1RA use between cancer and noncancer cohorts with and without adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics and comorbidities and diabetes-related complications; (2) cancer-specific factors associated with GLP-1RA use among the cancer cohort after 2018. A total of 373 278 Medicare beneficiaries (mean [SD] age, 76.1 [6.6] years; 188 746 [50.6%] female) with cancer and diabetes and 373 278 noncancer controls (153 358 unique beneficiaries) were included. GLP-1 RA use increased from 85 beneficiaries (0.5%) to 9083 beneficiaries (8.2%) and from 138 beneficiaries (0.9%) to 9300 beneficiaries (6.2%) in the cancer and noncancer cohorts, respectively, from 2010 to 2022 under TM; a similar increase was observed under MA. Despite higher unadjusted GLP-1 RA use among the cancer cohort than the noncancer cohort (probability difference, TM: 1.19 [95% CI, 0.94 to 1.44] percentage points [pp]; P < .001; MA: 0.45 [95% CI, 0.21 to 0.68] pp, P < .001), adjusted analysis showed no significant differences in GLP-1 RA use under TM (adjusted probability difference, 0.16 [95% CI, -0.10 to 0.41,] pp; P = .22) and lower use among cancer cohort under MA (-0.52 [95% CI, -0.76 to -0.28] pp; P < .001). Complications or comorbidities, including obesity (adjusted probability difference, TM: 3.35 [95% CI, 3.10 to 3.61] pp; P < .001; MA: 2.42 [95% CI, 2.19 to 2.64] pp; P < .001), dyslipidemia (adjusted probability difference, TM: 2.26 [95% CI, 2.03 to 2.50] pp; P < .001; MA: 1.80 [95% CI, 1.57 to 2.03] pp; P < .001), neuropathy (adjusted probability difference: TM: 3.91 [95% CI, 3.64 to 4.19] pp; P < .001; MA: 3.17 [95% CI, 2.94 to 3.41] pp; P < .001), retinopathy (adjusted probability difference, TM: 2.02 [95% CI, 1.78 to 2.27] pp; P < .001; MA: 1.84 [95% CI, 1.63 to 2.06] pp; P < .001), and chronic kidney disease (adjusted probability difference, TM: 2.01 [95% CI, 1.76 to 2.26] pp; P < .001; MA: 1.63 [95% CI, 1.40 to 1.85] pp; P < .001) were associated with greater likelihood of GLP-1RA use. Within the cancer cohort, breast (adjusted probability difference, TM: 1.05 [95% CI, 0.43 to 1.66] pp; P = .001; MA: 0.89 [95% CI, 0.37 to 1.41] pp; P = .001), gynecologic (adjusted probability difference, MA: 1.13 [95% CI, 0.45 to 1.81] pp; P = .001), and prostate (adjusted probability difference, TM: 1.30 [95% CI, 0.72 to 1.88] pp; P < .001; MA: 1.07 [95% CI, 0.56 to 1.58] pp; P < .001) cancers were associated with higher GLP-1 RA use than colorectal cancer, while pancreatic cancer was associated with lower GLP-1 RA use (adjusted probability difference, TM: -2.55 [95% CI, -3.17 to -1.93] pp; P < .001; MA: -1.64 [95% CI, -2.23 to -1.05] pp; P < .001). In this retrospective study of Medicare beneficiaries with type 2 diabetes, GLP-1 RA use increased substantially and primarily was associated with metabolic risk profile, with limited associations with cancer status. Variation across cancer types and stages suggests oncologic context may influence prescribing.

title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Therapy in Patients with Cancer: A Review of Clinical Outcomes.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are increasingly used for the management of obesity and type 2 diabetes, including among patients with cancer. Although previous research has mainly focused on cancer incidence, their associations with clinical outcomes after cancer diagnosis remain less well characterized. Therefore, the present study aimed to evaluate the oncologic and survival outcomes associated with GLP-1 RA use in adults with an established malignancy. We performed a systematic review of comparative studies evaluating GLP-1 RA use in patients with a confirmed cancer diagnosis. PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science were searched for English-language publications from 1 January 2016 to 8 August 2026. Twenty-six retrospective cohort studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. Thirteen studies included selective GLP-1 RAs and tirzepatide within the same exposure group. Study quality was assessed using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Twenty-five studies evaluated overall survival and/or all-cause mortality, while nine assessed cancer recurrence, progression, or related outcomes. Survival and mortality outcomes more often favored the exposed group (especially compared with nonuse) than not, but findings were less consistent in active-comparator analyses. Evidence for recurrence and progression was sparse and heterogeneous, and no clear signal of increased risk was observed. Because all of these were observational studies with substantial differences in populations, comparators, exposure definitions, and duration of follow-up, the survival associations do not imply causality or direct antitumor effects of GLP-1 RAs. Clinically, the preponderance of evidence does not support the use of GLP-1 RAs as cancer-directed therapy, and their use in patients with cancer should be guided by established indications such as obesity and type 2 diabetes. Potential explanations include effects on glycemic and cardiovascular risk factors, treatment selection, residual confounding, or combinations thereof. Prospective studies and randomized controlled trials with cancer-specific outcomes and longer follow-up are needed to further evaluate these associations.

title: Body Weight Changes and Exploratory Metabolic Outcomes During Semaglutide and Tirzepatide Treatment: A Real-World Longitudinal Cohort Study from Türkiye.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Comparative real-world evidence on early body-weight changes during semaglutide and tirzepatide treatment remains limited, particularly in populations with unequal and irregularly timed follow-up. To compare longitudinal percentage changes in body weight between adults initiating semaglutide and those initiating tirzepatide and to describe changes in anthropometric measures, weight-loss responses, and exploratory metabolic outcomes. Methods: This retrospective, single-center, real-world longitudinal cohort study included adults aged ≥18 years initiating semaglutide or tirzepatide for weight management, with a body mass index (BMI) ≥30 kg/m2 or ≥27 kg/m2 with a weight-related comorbidity. Patients with type 2 diabetes and concomitant obesity were eligible. Participants were naïve to incretin-based therapy; pregnancy, previous bariatric surgery, and active malignancy were exclusion criteria. Anthropometric and laboratory data were extracted from clinical records. Percentage body-weight change over days 1-230 was analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model incorporating exact follow-up time and adjusting for age, sex, baseline BMI, and diabetes status. Scheduled-visit and sensitivity analyses were also performed. Results: The cohort included 184 patients: 94 (51.1%) receiving semaglutide and 90 (48.9%) receiving tirzepatide. Overall, mean age was 41.7 ± 12.0 years, baseline weight was 97.0 ± 17.9 kg, and 139 patients (75.5%) were female. The longitudinal analysis included 345 measurements from 148 patients (80.4%). The treatment-by-time interaction was significant (p = 0.002). Adjusted weight changes with semaglutide versus tirzepatide were -3.39% versus -4.44% at month 1 (p = 0.116), -8.38% versus -11.52% at month 3 (p < 0.001), and -14.40% versus -15.06% at month 6 (p = 0.699). Sensitivity analyses yielded consistent findings. Only four tirzepatide-treated patients had measurements within the month 6 visit window; therefore, the month 6 estimate for this group relied primarily on the model and requires cautious interpretation. Conclusions: Both semaglutide and tirzepatide were associated with early reductions in body weight. Tirzepatide was associated with larger model-adjusted weight loss at month 3 (between-group difference, -3.14 percentage points; 95% CI, -4.55 to -1.74; p < 0.001), whereas no statistically significant between-group difference was observed at month 1 (p = 0.116). Only four tirzepatide-treated patients had measurements within the month 6 visit window, limiting the reliability of this comparison. Longer-term comparisons require cohorts with more balanced follow-up and more observations at later time points.

title: Semaglutide, Other GLP-1 Receptor Agonists, and Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma: A Narrative Review of Risk, Progression, and Mechanisms.
abstract: Semaglutide, a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA), is widely prescribed for type 2 diabetes and obesity. Rodent studies showed thyroid C-cell tumors, prompting a boxed warning for medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC); whether this extends to papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC), a follicular-cell-derived tumor, is uncertain. This narrative review examines semaglutide and other GLP-1RAs in relation to PTC, distinguishing semaglutide-specific from class-level evidence, and PTC from differentiated thyroid cancer (DTC), MTC, and thyroid cancer overall. Most human studies evaluated GLP-1RAs as a class and reported thyroid cancer overall; semaglutide-specific and PTC-specific estimates are scarce. Pooled trials and national cohorts mostly showed no statistically significant increase in thyroid cancer, although three separate meta-analyses of randomized trials each reported a statistically significant increase in overall thyroid cancer, and case-control and spontaneous-reporting studies reported signals vulnerable to detection bias and confounding. In a matched cohort of 1072 patients with DTC, GLP-1RA exposure (median 16 months) was not significantly associated with progression over 69 months. Receptor-expression findings were inconsistent, and preclinical data did not show proliferative effects. The cohort and progression findings indicate no statistically detectable increase within the available sample sizes, exposure durations, and event numbers; they do not establish oncological safety. Semaglutide-specific, histology-resolved studies with longer exposure are needed.

title: Signature Definition Shapes Associations Between Exenatide-Related Transcriptional Programs and Macrophage Senescence Scores in Colorectal Cancer.
abstract: Background: Treatment-derived expression signatures are often applied to untreated tumor cohorts, although their biological meaning may depend on signature construction and cellular composition. We examined the relationship between an exenatide-derived signature and senescence-associated macrophage expression in colorectal cancer. Methods: Archived pan-cancer and patient-level results were examined alongside a reconstruction from public mouse bulk RNA sequencing and colorectal single-cell matrices. Exenatide signatures were re-derived with tissue and batch adjustment, within-mouse correlation, and one-to-one orthologue mapping. Shared-gene removal, stricter macrophage annotation, expression-matched random signatures, virtual perturbation summaries, and three murine treatment comparisons assessed interpretation and robustness. Results: The original signature was associated with SenMayo in stomach, colon, and rectal tumor analyses. Reconstruction retained 209,207 colorectal cells and 4316 tumor macrophages, with 17 patients eligible for tumor-level analysis. Removing CXCR2 and IL1B from both signatures preserved a positive association (Spearman ρ = 0.804; adjusted β = 1.526; p = 0.00219). The corresponding mean expression association exceeded most expression-matched random signatures (empirical p = 0.006). Associations persisted with a blocked log-expression derivation but were absent with a blocked voom-derived signature using one-to-one orthologues (ρ = 0.056; p = 0.620). Archived virtual IL1B deletion and overexpression predicted opposing shifts after multiplicity adjustment. Treatment-macrophage fold-change correlations remained small (ρ = -0.038 to 0.046), with heterogeneous enrichment. The association was attenuated after adjustment for either inflammatory score-it remained statistically detectable after TNFα/NF-κB adjustment (β = 0.672, 95% CI 0.307-1.037) and was less precisely estimated after broader inflammatory response adjustment (β = 0.383, 95% CI -0.031-0.797). Conclusions: The original exenatide-derived signature was associated with SenMayo scores in colorectal tumor macrophages after removal of shared genes. This association overlapped with inflammatory expression and varied with signature derivation. Dependence on signature derivation limits its interpretation as a pharmacological response marker. These findings support investigation of inflammatory macrophage states without establishing drug-induced senescence.

title: Obesity-driven inflammation and immune dysregulation in cancer development and progression.
abstract: Obesity increases the risk and progression of at least 13 types of cancer. Although the epidemiologic links between excess adiposity and these cancers are well documented, the biological mechanisms linking obesity to carcinogenesis and tumor progression remain incompletely understood. White adipose tissue in obesity is a source of inflammatory and immunosuppressive signals that act systemically, driving metabolic, inflammatory, and immune dysfunction whose consequences differ across tumor types. As adipose tissue expands and adipocytes enlarge, the blood supply becomes inadequate, leading to hypoxia, fibrosis, lipolytic stress, macrophage recruitment, and chronic low-grade inflammation. These obesity-induced perturbations generate endocrine, cytokine, lipid, and metabolic signals that act systemically, within the tumor microenvironment (TME), and/or cell-intrinsically to activate oncogenic and tumor-promoting pathways. The same signals reshape innate and adaptive immunity, promoting tumor-permissive macrophage states and myeloid-derived suppressor cell expansion, while the effector arms weaken as antigen presentation, natural killer cell and T cell function all decline. This review synthesizes current evidence linking obesity-associated inflammation and immune dysregulation to cancer initiation, progression, and treatment responses across multiple obesity-related cancers. Emphasis is placed on adipose tissue inflammation, myeloid cell biology, T cell immunometabolism, endocrine-inflammatory crosstalk, and the relationship between obesity and immunotherapy. Finally, we discuss translational opportunities for preventing or intercepting obesity-related cancers, including weight loss achieved through lifestyle, surgical, or pharmacologic approaches, with an emphasis on GLP-1 receptor agonists given their substantial efficacy, rapid clinical uptake, and potential to reshape obesity-related cancer prevention and survivorship strategies. Defining the metabolic, immune, and inflammatory phenotypes that drive obesity-associated cancer risk and progression will be essential for developing more precise, mechanism-based strategies for prevention, treatment, and survivorship care.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists and adverse outcomes in patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic viral hepatitis.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RA) are a novel class of anti-diabetic drugs that can treat obesity and type 2 diabetes (T2D). T2D and chronic viral hepatitis (CVH) frequently coexist and worsen liver and non-liver outcomes, but effective pharmacological therapies are limited. We aimed to evaluate the effect of GLP-1RA on liver and non-liver complications among patients with T2D and CVH in the United States. Patients with T2D and CVH initiating GLP-1RA were included (2013-2022) in Merative™ Marketscan® Research Databases. Primary outcomes included (1) hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and cirrhosis, and (2) cardiovascular disease (CVD), chronic kidney disease (CKD), and non-liver cancer. Cox proportional hazards models were conducted to estimate hazard ratio (HR) and 95% confidence interval (CI). A total of 9,499 patients with T2D and CVH were included after 1:4 propensity score matching. Compared with non-GLP-1RA (N=7,366), GLP-1RA use (N=2,133) was associated with significantly lower risks of any liver-related outcomes (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.57-0.87; P=0.001), HCC (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.31-0.93; P=0.028), cirrhosis (HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.56-0.86; P<0.001), CKD (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.53-0.84; P<0.001). A trend toward a lower risk of CVD (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.66-1.03; P=0.089) and non-liver cancer (HR 0.73, 95% CI 0.53-1.01; P=0.055) was observed among GLP-1RA users, although the association did not reach statistical significance. GLP-1RA use was associated with lower risks of cirrhosis, HCC, and CKD among patients with T2D and CVH, with nonsignificant trends toward lower risks of CVD and non-liver cancer.

title: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist use and risk of postmastectomy lymphedema in breast cancer survivors: a multicenter real-world cohort study.
journal: Supportive care in cancer : official journal of the Multinational Association of Supportive Care in Cancer
abstract: Postmastectomy lymphedema is a chronic survivorship complication after breast cancer treatment, particularly among patients exposed to axillary surgery. Obesity and metabolic inflammation are recognized contributors to lymphedema risk. This study evaluated whether glucagon-like peptide - 1 receptor agonist exposure was associated with lower incidence of coded postmastectomy lymphedema among breast cancer patients with mastectomy and/or axillary procedure exposure. We performed a retrospective cohort study using deidentified electronic health record data from the TriNetX Research Network. Adult patients with breast cancer and coded mastectomy and/or axillary procedural exposure were stratified by GLP-1 receptor agonist exposure versus no exposure. One-to-one propensity score matching was used to balance measured baseline characteristics. The primary outcome was incident coded postmastectomy lymphedema syndrome. Outcomes were assessed from 1 to 650 days after the index event using risk estimates, Kaplan-Meier analysis, and Cox proportional hazards models. After propensity score matching, 61,630 patients were included, with 30,815 patients in each cohort. Coded postmastectomy lymphedema occurred in 258 of 29,259 GLP-1 receptor agonist users and 779 of 30,237 non-users, corresponding to incidence rates of 0.88% and 2.58%, respectively. GLP-1 receptor agonist exposure was associated with lower incidence of coded postmastectomy lymphedema in time-to-event analysis (hazard ratio 0.373, 95% CI 0.324-0.429; p < 0.001). The absolute risk difference was - 1.7%, with an estimated number needed to treat of 59. In this large real-world breast cancer surgical/procedural cohort, GLP-1 receptor agonist exposure was associated with lower incidence of coded postmastectomy lymphedema over 650 days of follow-up. These findings are hypothesis-generating and require prospective validation with systematic lymphedema assessment and detailed characterization of GLP-1 receptor agonist timing, duration, dose, and adherence.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonist-associated weight loss in breast cancer patients receiving concurrent endocrine therapy: a retrospective cohort analysis.
abstract: Endocrine therapy for hormone receptor-positive breast cancer is associated with adverse metabolic effects - including increased fat mass, decreased lean muscle mass, and insulin resistance - that may attenuate the efficacy of GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs). This study evaluated GLP-1 RA-associated weight loss outcomes in breast cancer patients receiving concurrent endocrine therapy. We conducted a retrospective cohort analysis of 269 breast cancer patients at a single academic center receiving concurrent GLP-1 RA and adjuvant endocrine therapy. GLP-1 RA and endocrine therapy data were obtained from electronic medication reconciliation lists and pharmacy dispense reports. Patients were required to have initiated GLP-1 therapy during the study period and to have received concurrent GLP-1 RA and endocrine therapy for at least one year. The primary outcome was percentage weight change from GLP-1 initiation to 12 months (± 2 months). Secondary outcomes included proportions achieving ≥ 5%, ≥ 10%, and ≥ 15% weight loss. Mean one-year percentage weight loss was - 4.5% (95% CI: -6.0% to - 3.0%; -3.9 kg; 95% CI: -4.96 to - 2.93 kg), significantly below the 10-20% observed in postmenopausal subgroups of GLP-1 randomized trials (all p < 0.001). Only 21.3% achieved ≥ 10% and 10.4% achieved ≥ 15% weight loss. Weight loss differed significantly by GLP-1 agent (p = 0.003); semaglutide (- 5.8%) and tirzepatide (- 4.7%) outperformed dulaglutide (+ 0.1%), which is approved for type 2 diabetes only. Higher baseline weight was associated with greater absolute loss (r = - 0.19, p = 0.002), though percentage weight loss did not differ significantly by baseline BMI category (p = 0.303). PR-negative patients lost more than PR-positive patients (- 8.2% vs. -4.2%; p = 0.021, d = 0.46). Type 2 diabetes was present in 70.6% of patients; T2DM status was not significantly associated with weight loss on t-test (p = 0.288), though patients without T2DM were numerically more likely to achieve ≥ 15% loss (21.5% vs. 5.8%). GLP-1 RAs produce statistically significant but substantially attenuated weight loss in breast cancer patients on concurrent endocrine therapy. GLP-1 agent selection significantly influences outcomes. Given emerging evidence of oncologic benefit, prospective trials are needed.

title: The Theory of the Patient: Toward an Integration of Clinical Reasoning, Causal Inference, and Mechanistic Biology.
journal: Journal of evaluation in clinical practice
abstract: Clinical medicine, epidemiology, and mechanistic biology each have partial purchase on disease, but none treats the patient (the individual biological system constituted by genetics, biography, environment, and time) as a unifying object of inquiry. Population-level causal inference cannot explain why a specific intervention failed in a specific patient. Cause is the language of populations; mechanism is the language of the individual. To propose a theory of the patient: a scientifically grounded account of how biological, biographical, and environmental processes interacted over time in this person to produce their disease and shape their response to treatment; and to show that it meets the criteria of a scientific theory. Conceptual analysis drawing on Peirce's and Lipton's accounts of abduction, mechanistic philosophy of science (Salmon; Machamer, Darden, and Craver), and the potential outcomes framework, applied to an illustrative case of treatment resistant breast cancer. The theory has three components. Abduction, inference to the best mechanistic explanation of a singular clinical course, is its epistemological foundation. The Mechanistic History Graph (MHG), an individualized, temporal, mechanistic representation whose configurations are competing hypotheses, is its formal structure. Bio-Biographical Mechanistic Profiling (BBMP), which reconstructs the biographical and biological dimensions that clinical science omits, is its empirical content. The MHG for the index case specifies three competing theories of resistance (acquired molecular resistance, biography-driven local aromatase bypass, and CDK4/6 pathway escape) and the evidence that would discriminate among them, testable prospectively by embedding BBMP and pre-specified interaction hypotheses in trials such as pionERA. The framework extends as illustration to darapladib, checkpoint inhibitors, and GLP-1 agonists. A theory of the patient explains, predicts, unifies, generates new observations, and is falsifiable. It complements rather than replaces population-level causal inference, providing a clinical science adequate to the individuality of the patient.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonists and lymphedema: from weight loss to potential direct modulation of lymphatic function.
abstract: Obesity and lymphedema are linked through increased interstitial fluid load, impaired collecting-vessel pumping, inflammation, and progressive fibro-adipose remodeling. This bidirectional relationship makes glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) relevant through two potentially distinct pathways. First, substantial weight loss may unload a compromised lymphatic system, improve mobility, and reduce adipose-driven inflammation. Second, GLP-1 signaling may directly influence lymphatic vessel function. Case reports and a retrospective cohort have described reduced limb volume, improved symptoms or imaging findings, and a lower incidence of breast cancer-related lymphedema among GLP-1RA users. Experimental work has identified GLP-1 receptors in lymphatic endothelial cells and shown that pharmacological activation with semaglutide increases the pumping capacity of isolated collecting lymphatic vessels. These findings support a potential direct lymphatic effect but do not establish clinical efficacy in human lymphedema. Improvement during treatment may instead reflect reduced fat mass, greater mobility, or changes in conventional care. Future studies should distinguish weight-loss-dependent unloading from weight-loss-independent effects by combining standardized clinical outcomes, functional imaging, body-composition measurements, and, where feasible, weight-matched comparison groups. The available evidence therefore supports prospective investigation rather than clinical adoption. Trials should assess early vascular responses before major weight loss, longer-term changes in tissue composition and inflammation, and durability after treatment withdrawal, while maintaining standardized compression, exercise, skin care, and other components of established lymphedema management throughout. Until such evidence is available, GLP-1RAs should be prescribed for established metabolic indications rather than lymphedema itself, and any lymphatic benefit should be regarded as a promising clinical signal rather than a treatment claim.

title: Metabolic dysfunctions in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma: Pathogenic mechanisms and therapeutic implications.
journal: Pancreatology : official journal of the International Association of Pancreatology (IAP) ... [et al.]
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains a highly aggressive malignancy characterized by a dismal prognosis and profound resistance to conventional therapies. Emerging evidence highlights systemic metabolic dysfunctions including obesity, dyslipidemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), and non-alcoholic fatty pancreatic disease (NAFPD) as critical drivers of PDAC initiation, progression and chemoresistance. This review integrates current knowledge on the intricate interplay between metabolic alterations and PDAC biology, focusing on the therapeutic and chemopreventive potential of repurposed metabolic modulators (specifically statins and antidiabetic agents) and novel metabolic pathway inhibitors currently under clinical evaluation. Statins exert prominent antitumor effects in preclinical models by disrupting the mevalonate pathway, impairing Ras prenylation, and reprogramming cholesterol metabolism; however, epidemiological data regarding risk reduction remain inconsistent. Parallel to lipid pathways, glucose homeostasis dictates tumor behavior. T2DM acts as both a potent risk factor and an early paraneoplastic indicator through new-onset diabetes. Among antidiabetic drugs, metformin attenuates PDAC progression via insulin-lowering and AMPK-mediated pathways, though its survival benefits are often obscured in clinical trials by methodological challenges. Conversely, hyperinsulinemia driven by exogenous insulin or secretagogues exacerbates PDAC risk, while incretin-based therapies yield conflicting outcomes. Notably, novel strategies targeting metabolic vulnerabilities, such as SGLT2 inhibition combined with metformin, show promise in targeting chemoresistant, nutrient-deprived tumor zones. Ultimately, integrating metabolic profiling, prescription history, and molecular biomarkers into clinical practice is essential to advance risk stratification and precision oncology. Overcoming tumor metabolic plasticity in contemporary clinical trials will require a shift from single-node therapies towards rational, biomarker-guided combination strategies.

title: Association of GLP-1 Receptor Agonist Use with Thyroid Outcomes in Adults with Type 2 Diabetes.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are widely used to treat type 2 diabetes mellitus, but their associations with thyroid disorders remain uncertain. We evaluated whether initiating a GLP-1 RA, compared with initiating a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitor (DPP-4i), was associated with newly recorded autoimmune thyroiditis and other thyroid outcomes. This new-user, active-comparator cohort study emulated a target trial using the TriNetX Collaborative Network. Adults with type 2 diabetes who initiated a GLP-1 RA or DPP-4i between January 1, 2018, and December 31, 2022, and had no prior use of either drug class were eligible. Patients with pre-existing thyroid disease, any neoplasm, immunosuppressant or immunostimulant use, transplantation, or end-stage kidney disease or dialysis were excluded. Propensity score matching yielded 107,912 patients per group. The primary outcome was newly recorded autoimmune thyroiditis; secondary outcomes were nontoxic uninodular goiter, nontoxic multinodular goiter, and thyroid malignancy. Cox models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs), with false discovery rate adjustment. Follow-up extended from 1 day after treatment initiation to 4 years. Autoimmune thyroiditis occurred in 524 GLP-1 RA users (0.49%) and 417 DPP-4i users (0.39%). GLP-1 RA initiation was associated with a higher risk of autoimmune thyroiditis (HR, 1.26; 95% CI, 1.11-1.43; FDR-adjusted P = 0.002). Modestly higher risks were also observed for nontoxic uninodular goiter (HR, 1.07; 95% CI, 1.01-1.13) and nontoxic multinodular goiter (HR, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.03-1.19). The risk of thyroid malignancy did not differ significantly (HR, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.77-1.12). Findings were generally consistent across sensitivity and subgroup analyses, although heterogeneity was observed across body mass index strata. Among adults with type 2 diabetes, GLP-1 RA initiation was associated with small increases in newly recorded autoimmune thyroiditis and benign nodular thyroid disease, but not with thyroid malignancy. Given the small absolute differences and the potential for residual confounding and surveillance bias, these findings require validation in future studies.

title: GLP-1 Receptor Agonists and Cancer Risk in Obesity Treatment.
journal: Obesity reviews : an official journal of the International Association for the Study of Obesity
abstract: Obesity is a well-established risk factor for numerous cancers, with body habitus, especially central adiposity, contributing to increased cancer incidence and worse prognosis. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs), initially developed to treat Type 2 diabetes, have rapidly gained prominence as powerful anti-obesity agents due to their ability to induce significant weight loss and potential to improve metabolic health. These medications act by reducing appetite, enhancing insulin sensitivity, lowering systemic inflammation, and preferentially targeting fat mass for reduction. This review explores the growing body of evidence linking GLP-1 RA therapy to potential changes in cancer risk among individuals with obesity. To date, data suggest that GLP-1 RAs do not increase overall cancer risk and may reduce the risk of certain obesity-related cancers, likely by interrupting obesity-driven metabolic dysregulation. Still, questions remain about the beneficial effects of weight loss and the sustainability of health benefits if weight is regained after stopping treatment. We examine how GLP-1 RAs' anti-inflammatory and metabolic effects might mediate reductions in cancer risk, review emerging data regarding both protective signals and specific safety concerns (e.g., increased risk of medullary thyroid carcinoma), and emphasize the critical role of combining pharmacotherapy with lifestyle interventions to maintain muscle mass and long-term weight loss. Ultimately, given the strong link between obesity and cancer, GLP-1 RAs represent a promising new class of agents that may not only help to manage obesity but also serve as effective chemopreventive tools against obesity-associated cancers.

title: A Dicyanocobinamide Conjugate of the GLP-1R Agonist Exendin-4 Improves Glucose Homeostasis in Tumor-Bearing Rats without Exacerbating Anorexia and Weight Loss.
abstract: Cancer anorexia-cachexia syndrome (CACS) is a prevalent and debilitating complication of malignancy, characterized by reduced food intake, loss of skeletal muscle mass, and severe metabolic dysfunction. Insulin resistance and impaired glucose tolerance are prominent features of CACS and contribute to worsened prognosis, yet treatment options that improve metabolic regulation without exacerbating anorexia are limited. Although GLP-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonists effectively enhance glucose control, their centrally mediated anorectic and aversive effects limit their use in cancer patients. To address this limitation, we developed a peripherally restricted GLP-1R agonist by conjugating exendin-4 (Ex4) to dicyanocobinamide (Cbi), a vitamin B12-derived corrin ring with minimal blood-brain barrier penetration. Here, we evaluate Cbi-Ex4 in vitro and across healthy and tumor-bearing rodent models. Cbi-Ex4 retained GLP-1R agonism and improved glucose tolerance without inducing anorexia, weight loss, or malaise, in contrast to native Ex4. These findings support peripheralized GLP-1R agonism as a promising strategy to improve metabolic dysfunction in cancer without worsening malaise and cachexia.

title: Decoding the Safety Profile of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists: Facts, Myths, and Ongoing Controversies.
abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1RAs) represent one of the most significant therapeutic advances in the management of type 2 diabetes and obesity. As their indications have expanded to include cardiovascular and kidney disease, safety concerns involving multiple organ systems have received increasing attention. This narrative review examines the spectrum of adverse effects linked to GLP-1RAs and provides a clinically relevant platform for assessing their safe prescription. Gastrointestinal intolerance, modest increases in heart rate, and a modest but reproducible increase in the risk of gallbladder and biliary disease represent the most consistently supported adverse effects of GLP-1RAs. A risk of pancreatitis is also considered to exist, although some studies have challenged this association. Conversely, correlations with neuropsychiatric and dermatological disorders, diabetic retinopathy, nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy, perioperative aspiration, sexual and reproductive disturbances, sarcopenia, and malignancy remain controversial. Most available evidence derives from pharmacovigilance databases, retrospective observational studies, and secondary analyses of randomized trials, which are limited by reporting bias, residual confounding, and inability to establish causality. Heterogeneity in study design, statistical methodology, outcome definitions, and patient populations further complicates interpretation. Although several proposed adverse effects have biologically plausible mechanisms, prospective clinical validation remains limited. Notably, recent regulatory decisions, including the Food and Drug Administration (FDA)'s removal of the suicidality warning from GLP-1RA prescribing information, reflect the evolving nature of these safety assessments. The overall benefit-risk profile of GLP-1RAs is favorable. Most emerging safety concerns should currently be regarded as hypothesis-generating signals rather than established toxicities. Individualized risk assessment and appropriate clinical monitoring remain important as ongoing and future prospective studies further define the long-term safety of this rapidly expanding therapeutic class.

title: Prevention Before Therapy in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma: The Clinical, Economic, and Human Case for Weighting Resources Upstream.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is projected to become the second-leading cause of US cancer death by 2030, and survival is dominated by stage at diagnosis: roughly 44% at five years for localized disease versus about 3% with distant metastases. Only about 15% of cases are detected while localized, surgery reaches a minority of patients, and no validated screening test exists for average-risk adults. This topical review examines the biologic, clinical, economic, psychological, equity, and therapeutic evidence bearing on where scarce resources should be directed. The long interval between initiating mutation and invasive disease provides a mechanistic rationale for prevention and interception, and the modifiable exposures of obesity, tobacco, type 2 diabetes, and alcohol act largely within that window. We consider innovations that extend prevention beyond lifestyle advice-incretin-based weight management, risk stratification anchored in new-onset diabetes and biomarkers, and immunoprevention-together with early-onset disease, implementation and policy, and the barriers and evidentiary limits that temper these arguments. We propose a three-tier framework of primary prevention, early detection in high-risk groups, and therapy, and argue that research, policy, and clinical investment should be weighted upstream, because every case prevented spares the cost, capacity, and suffering that the downstream tiers must otherwise absorb.

title: GLP-1R agonism in breast cancer: a metabolic-oncogenic switch?
Evaluating the safety of glucagon-like peptide-1 agonist use in non-diabetic overweight patients undergoing shoulder arthroplasty.
journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow arthroplasty
abstract: Initially indicated for diabetes mellitus (DM), glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) agonists are now indicated for obesity management in isolation of DM. While prior studies have examined post-operative outcomes after total shoulder arthroplasty (TSA) in GLP-1 users with DM, there is a paucity of literature evaluating its use in non-diabetic patients for weight loss rather than glucose control. Therefore, our analysis compared 90-day and 2-year outcomes following TSA between non-diabetic obese GLP-1 users and a matched cohort of obese GLP-1 non-users. The PearlDiver Mariner database was queried to identify patients who underwent anatomic TSA and reverse TSA between 2010 and 2023. Patients with a history of DM or who underwent TSA for cancer, infection, or pathologic fractures were excluded. Patients with a body mass index ≥ 30 kg/m2 within 6 months of surgery were included. GLP-1 users (within 3 months of surgery) were matched in a 1:10 ratio to GLP-1 non-users by age, sex, Elixhauser Comorbidity Index, smoking status, and various comorbidities. Multivariate logistic regression models were utilized to compare outcomes at 90 days and 2 years. After matching, 462 GLP-1 users and 4,377 GLP-1 non-users were included in our analysis. GLP-1 users had higher readmission rates (odds ratio: 2.034; 95% confidence interval: 1.594-2.578; P < .001) and subsequently overall complication rates (odds ratio: 1.474; 95% confidence interval: 1.295-1.799; P < .001) compared to GLP-1 non-users at 90 days. However, no differences were seen between cohorts for the remaining 90-day outcomes nor for all evaluated 2-year outcomes including prosthetic joint infection, fracture, and all-cause revision. Our analysis found a higher incidence of overall complications at 90 days among obese, non-diabetic GLP-1 users, driven largely by an increased incidence of readmissions. However, there were largely comparable outcomes at 2 years. These findings suggest that while GLP-1 agonists may be reasonable to use in the perioperative period, interventions to reduce readmissions among these patients may be warranted.

title: CagriSema versus Semaglutide 2.4 mg monotherapy for weight management in adults with overweight or obesity, with or without type 2 diabetes: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and trial sequential analysis.
abstract: Semaglutide 2.4 mg is the reference pharmacotherapy for weight management, yet many patients do not reach ambitious weight-loss targets. CagriSema, a fixed-dose combination of cagrilintide and semaglutide, may offer additional benefit through complementary mechanisms. We quantified its incremental efficacy and safety against semaglutide 2.4 mg monotherapy in adults with overweight or obesity, with and without type 2 diabetes. This PRISMA 2020-compliant review (PROSPERO CRD420261380458) searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, ScienceDirect, ClinicalTrials.gov and WHO ICTRP to 30 June 2026 for randomised controlled trials comparing CagriSema with semaglutide 2.4 mg or placebo. Effects were pooled within two prespecified comparator strata using random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation of τ² and a Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman small-sample adjustment, with prediction intervals, leave-one-out and phase-3a-restricted sensitivity analyses, trial sequential analysis. Five trials (4,746 unique participants) were included. Versus semaglutide 2.4 mg, CagriSema produced greater weight loss (mean difference -6.89 percentage points, 95% CI -8.70 to -5.06; I² = 33%; prediction interval -8.91 to -4.86), a greater absolute reduction in body weight (-7.16 kg, 95% CI -9.15 to -5.17) and in body-mass index (-2.41 kg/m², 95% CI -2.83 to -1.99), and roughly twice the likelihood of reaching a 20% reduction (RR 2.10, 95% CI 1.78 to 2.47). Waist circumference fell further (-4.07 cm, 95% CI -5.10 to -3.04). No incremental glycaemic benefit was detected, with intervals for glycated haemoglobin (-0.07, 95% CI -0.14 to 0.01) and fasting plasma glucose lying entirely within prespecified minimal important differences. Injection-site reactions were more frequent (RR 3.14, 95% CI 1.42 to 6.96); gastrointestinal adverse events were not significantly increased under the primary model (RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.21). CagriSema produces clinically meaningful additional weight loss and modest improvements in surrogate cardiometabolic measures compared with semaglutide 2.4 mg alone, at the cost of more frequent injection-site reactions and, at most, modestly more frequent gastrointestinal events. The evidence is insufficient to determine whether serious adverse events or neoplasms differ between treatments, and long-term durability, cardiovascular outcomes and body composition remain undetermined. https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/, identifier CRD420261380458.

title: Recurrent In-Stent Restenosis and Accelerated Neoatherosclerosis in a Middle-Aged Woman With High Inflammatory Burden.
abstract: Recurrent in-stent restenosis (ISR) driven by accelerated neoatherosclerosis and high residual inflammatory risk remains a formidable clinical challenge. A 50-year-old noncompliant, obese, diabetic woman presented with recurrent multivessel ISR. Intravascular ultrasound confirmed intrastent thin-cap fibroatheromas. Despite multiple drug-coated balloon interventions, intensive lipid-lowering via inclisiran, and glycemic control with tirzepatide, she suffered relentless ISR driven by highly elevated interleukin-6. She received advanced anti-inflammatory therapies and was referred for bypass surgery. Literature highlights that targeting upstream inflammation is critical when standard therapies fail to halt malignant neoatherosclerosis. This case interests readers by demonstrating compliance optimization via long-acting agents and navigating advanced anti-inflammatory pathways (colchicine escalation, canakinumab) for refractory ISR. Biomarkers like interleukin-6 must be evaluated in refractory ISR; persistent residual inflammation warrants advanced anti-inflammatory therapies or early surgical revascularization.

title: Type 2 diabetes medications and their implications for cancer treatment: A comprehensive review.
abstract: The increasing prevalence of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) represents a significant public health challenge with serious implications for cancer incidence and treatment. Currently affecting over 400 million individuals worldwide, T2DM is characterized by chronic hyperglycemia and insulin resistance, which contribute to a pro-tumorigenic environment. This review seeks to elucidate the complex relationship between diabetes medications and cancer treatment, emphasizing how various agents, including metformin, sulfonylureas, dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists, thiazolidinediones (TZDs), and sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, interact with critical signaling pathways involved in cancer progression. Evidence suggests that these medications can modulate oncogenic pathways such as AMPK/mTOR, insulin/IGF signaling, and Nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB), leading to either inhibition or stimulation of tumor growth and survival depending on the drug class and biological context. For instance, metformin activates AMPK, inhibiting mTOR and promoting apoptosis, while TZDs exert anti-inflammatory effects that may reduce obesity-related cancer risks. Conversely, some DPP-4 inhibitors have been associated with pro-tumorigenic effects under certain conditions. Given the intricate interplay among diabetes, obesity, and cancer, understanding the effects of antidiabetic therapies on tumor biology is crucial for refining treatment strategies. This review consolidates current findings on the cellular and molecular impacts of major T2DM drug classes on cancer, highlighting their potential benefits and limitations. In conclusion, the findings presented in this analysis are intended to enhance treatment strategies and shape future research initiatives aimed at effectively addressing the complexities of managing patients who are concurrently affected by diabetes and cancer.

title: Research trends and knowledge structure of pancreatic cancer and type 2 diabetes mellitus research: a two-decade CiteSpace analysis.
abstract: Pancreatic cancer and type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) are closely linked through complex epidemiological and biological interactions.
